subject: Re: Tool-calling integration patterns — SDK setup, auth, routing, embeddings
messages:

Subject: Tool-calling integration: recap & questions

Marissa — great call today, thanks for walking through Redwood's runtime and the tool/function calling examples. Quick recap from our side and a few asks so we can prep for the next session: 

- What we heard: define tools (APIs) + structured output from the LLM, runtime routes calls to the correct tool, handle retries/errors, and post-process outputs into our systems.
- Our primary integration needs: SDK setup (server-side + browser), auth patterns (we need user-scoped access for some actions), routing to internal services vs 3rd-party tools, embeddings + reranking for search, and clear error handling strategies.

Could you share: a short prioritized checklist for integration, sample tool definitions we can review, and any recommended auth patterns for user-scoped flows vs server-to-server? Also: is there a reference architecture diagram you can send?

Propose a follow-up engineering deep-dive next week with your devs (Dev, Neha) — Wed/Thu mornings PT work best for us.

Thanks,
Sarah Bloom
Head of Integrations, FinApps Inc.
[sarah.bloom@finapps.com]

Subject: Re: Tool-calling integration: recap & next steps

Sarah — thanks, and great meeting. Recap + next steps below. Forwarding to our engineering SMEs (Dev & Neha) for a short technical deep-dive and samples.

Recap (short):
- Pattern: model returns a structured JSON payload (we recommend JSON Schema for validation). The payload includes a top-level "tool" field and a tool-specific "args" object. Redwood's runtime can either call the tool synchronously (for low-latency internal actions) or queue an async job for long-running ops.
- Tool defs: treat tools as typed interfaces (name, inputs schema, outputs schema, safe-side effects). We attached a sample set (sample-tool-defs.json).
- Routing: we suggest a policy-driven router: match tool name + context -> route (internal service / 3rd-party). Fallback: if a tool is unavailable, route to a compatible variant or return structured error for UI fallback.
- Structured output / errors: prefer a canonical envelope: { status: success|error, result: {...}, error: {code,message,retryable} } so clients can reliably handle errors. Include validation at the runtime edge to avoid downstream crashes.
- Embeddings & rerankers: two-step retrieval: candidate gen (ANN) -> rerank with cross-encoder or small LLM scoring. Cache embeddings and reuse where possible.

Attachments (attached): redwood-tool-calling-arch.pdf (reference architecture), sample-tool-defs.json (example tool schemas), auth-snippets.txt (short samples).

Proposed next steps:
1) Engineering deep-dive (45m): Dev & Neha to walk auth choices, routing, and embeddings. Wed/Thu mornings PT — propose Thu 2026-03-04 09:30 PT.
2) Share a 1-page prioritized checklist (we'll send this by EOD).
3) Provide sample tool definitions you can validate against your infra (attached).

Notes on auth (high-level):
- Server-to-server: API keys or mTLS for internal services + short-lived tokens issued by Redwood's control plane.
- User-scoped actions: OAuth2 (recommended) or delegated JWTs; Redwood can broker OAuth flows in Private deployments and exchange user tokens for short-lived credentials to call tools. Dev will detail patterns in the deep-dive.

Let us know if Thu 03/04 09:30 PT works.

—

Sarah — quick technical notes ahead of the deep-dive.

Auth patterns:
- For user-scoped external services we should use OAuth2 with Redwood acting as a broker (if you want us to manage tokens) or pass-through if you manage users. Exchange flow: user authorizes -> Redwood receives short-lived token -> runtime signs tool calls with ephemeral creds (rotate every X minutes via KMS).
- For internal server-to-server, prefer short-lived JWTs signed by KMS (no long-lived static keys). Use key rotation and short TTLs (5-15m) for tool execution tokens.

Tool execution & routing:
- Define each tool with metadata: concurrency_limit, timeout_ms, idempotency_key (recommended). This helps runtime decide parallel vs sequential calls.
- Parallel tools: allowed if tools are independent and side-effect free; block/serialize if tools mutate the same resource. Use a policy engine to enforce.
- Error handling: classify errors as transient (retryable), permanent (no retry), or user-action-required. Runtime should return the canonical error envelope Marissa described.

Attachments: small auth snippet and a sample policy file included. I'll demo token exchange and a minimal client SDK snippet in the call.

—Dev
Dev Patel
Senior Backend Engineer, Redwood Inference

High-level on embeddings & reranking (for FinApps search flow):

- Candidate generation: use a dense-retrieval index built on sentence-transformer style embeddings (we recommend our curated "rw-embed-large-v1" for semantic recall). Persist embeddings in an ANN store (Pinecone/FAISS/Weaviate).
- Reranker: after retrieving top-N candidates, run a lightweight cross-encoder or a few-shot LLM scoring pass. This improves precision for user-facing results.
- Cost trade-offs: run reranker only on top 10-50 candidates; use batching for embeddings (our batch endpoint) to reduce per-call cost. Cache top results for frequent queries and warm KV caches where possible.
- Eval: bring a small prompt/eval set so we can measure P@k and tune thresholds — we'll include a suggested eval checklist in the one-pager.

I'll prepare a short benchmark comparison (embed size vs latency) and include recommended thresholds for your catalog.

—Neha
Neha Kapoor
Applied ML, Redwood Inference
